case.why_ai_cites_it: The principal authority that collecting public web data is not a federal computer crime, which is the first hurdle any web-scale training corpus has to clear.

reading.body:
hiQ Labs v. LinkedIn, a 2022 case holding that scraping publicly available website data without logging in does not violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, is described as the first hurdle any web-scale AI training corpus has to clear, and it is cited in defense in both Amazon.com Services lawsuits against Perplexity AI tracked here.

It shares those same two cases with Van Buren v. United States elsewhere in this collection, both CFAA precedents used together, which suggests the CFAA theory specifically has already been substantially closed off as an avenue against AI scraping practices, leaving other legal theories to carry the weight instead.

The case's own stated limit says exactly which theories remain. The CFAA holding leaves contract, trespass to chattels, copyright, and state privacy claims fully available, and the record notes that LinkedIn itself later prevailed against hiQ on contract grounds specifically, meaning the win described here was narrower than a full defense against all scraping-related claims.
